stories.head: Joshua Wong jailed for 10 more years for foreign collusion
stories.say: Hong Kong democracy activist Joshua Wong was sentenced on Thursday to ten more years in prison for conspiring to collude with foreign forces, his second national security conviction.
stories.stand: A Hong Kong court sentenced the pro-democracy activist under the 2020 national security law, his second conviction under it.
body: A Hong Kong court sentenced pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong to 10 years in prison on Thursday for conspiring to collude with foreign forces.

Prosecutors said that in 2020, after the 2019 anti-government protests, Wong asked foreign countries to impose sanctions or other measures on Hong Kong or China. He pleaded guilty in September, according to an EFE report carried by Infobae.
It is his second conviction under the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020. ABC News reported he had already served four years and eight months for subversion under the same law.
Wong, 30, rose to international prominence during the 2014 Umbrella Movement protests.

stories.head: Mother and daughter killed in suspected grizzly attack in Canada
stories.say: A mother and her 20-year-old daughter have been killed in a suspected grizzly bear attack near Bella Coola in British Columbia, and officials say more than one bear may be involved.
stories.stand: The two women's remains were found near Bella Coola, British Columbia; officials say it is unclear whether more than one bear was involved.
body: A mother and her 20-year-old daughter have died in a suspected grizzly bear attack near Bella Coola, British Columbia, Canadian officials said.

The pair went missing after a walk on the Snooka West Trail and were reported missing on Sunday. The mother's body was found on Monday and her daughter's remains on Tuesday, CBS News and Fox News reported.

Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the BC Conservation Officer Service, said it was not yet clear whether more than one bear was involved. Officers are trying to capture any bears involved, which will be put down under provincial guidelines.
People have been told to avoid the trail. A grizzly attacked a school group in the same area less than a year ago.

stories.head: Toll from Russian strike on Ukrainian aid centre rises to 40
stories.say: Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday that 40 people are now known to have died in Monday's Russian bombing of an aid centre in Komyshuvakha, with more than 30 possibly still under rubble.
stories.stand: Zelensky says more than 30 people may still be under the rubble of the school in Komyshuvakha that was being used to hand out aid.
body: President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday that the death toll from Monday's Russian strike on Komyshuvakha, in Zaporizhzhia region, had risen to 40.

The bombs hit a school building used to distribute humanitarian aid. Al Jazeera reported that a follow-up strike hit an underground shelter, and that four police officers and two rescuers were among the dead.
Zelensky said more than 30 people may still be under the rubble, and renewed calls for air defence. Russia's defence ministry said it had targeted Ukrainian military personnel, CBS News reported.
Separately, Zelensky said Melania Trump would receive Ukraine's Order of Princess Olga for brokering a temporary ceasefire to allow aid and evacuations in occupied Oleshky.

stories.head: Hungary opens communist-era secret police files to the public
stories.say: Hungary has put communist-era secret police records online for the first time, letting people search tens of thousands of names recorded by the state security services.
stories.stand: An online database lists tens of thousands of people recorded by the state security services, fulfilling a pledge by Péter Magyar's government.
body: Hungary has made communist-era secret police records searchable online for the first time. The database launched on Wednesday, the 70th anniversary of the Soviet crushing of the 1956 revolution.
The records come from the Historical Archives of the State Security Services. Daily News Hungary reported that one database lists about 55,000 people with code names and recruitment file numbers.
Historians warn that appearing in the records does not prove someone was an informer. Reports written by informers will not be published, to protect the privacy of those watched.
The release fulfils a campaign pledge by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, whose Tisza party ended Viktor Orbán's 16 years in power in April. Around 9,000 recruitment files are due by 25 February 2027.

stories.head: Bavarian deputy premier Hubert Aiwanger found dead in Berlin hotel
stories.say: Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria's deputy premier and leader of the Free Voters, has been found dead in a Berlin hotel aged 55; prosecutors are investigating and the cause is not yet known.
stories.stand: Berlin prosecutors are investigating the death of the 55-year-old Free Voters leader; the cause is not yet known.
body: Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria's deputy premier and economy minister, has been found dead in a Berlin hotel room at the age of 55.
He had cancelled an appearance at the opening of a Free Voters office in Berlin, citing health reasons, and later could not be reached, the dpa news agency reported.
Berlin prosecutors have opened an investigation into the cause and circumstances of his death, including ruling out the involvement of others. The cause is not yet known.
Bavarian premier Markus Söder called the death an absolute tragedy. Aiwanger led the Free Voters, which have governed Bavaria in coalition with Söder's CSU since 2018.

stories.head: Bukele warns Haiti's gangs as Salvadoran troops hunt for missing men
stories.say: Nayib Bukele has warned Haiti's gangs his forces can defeat them, as about 2,000 Salvadoran troops search for four compatriots missing since an ambush on 18 October.
stories.stand: El Salvador has sent about 2,000 troops to Haiti after four Salvadorans serving with a UN-backed force went missing in an ambush.
body: El Salvador's president, Nayib Bukele, has warned Haiti's gang leaders that his forces can defeat them, as he says they did in El Salvador.

El Salvador has deployed about 2,000 troops after four Salvadoran military personnel serving with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force went missing following an ambush near Port-au-Prince on 18 October.

Haitian police said on Tuesday they had found the burned vehicle in Croix-des-Bouquets, but no sign of the men. Bukele posted video he said showed Salvadoran helicopters firing on gangs attacking force soldiers from Chad.
Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé said the foreign forces had come to support the state, not replace it. The UN says El Salvador's operations must follow international law.

stories.head: Syria and Saudi Arabia sign defence deal and $403m in loans
stories.say: Syria and Saudi Arabia have signed a defence cooperation deal in Riyadh, along with $403m in Saudi loans for health, housing, civil defence and power projects.
stories.stand: President Ahmed al-Sharaa signed the agreements in Riyadh on his second visit in less than a month; the defence terms were not disclosed.
body: Syria and Saudi Arabia signed a defence cooperation agreement in Riyadh on Wednesday, during talks between Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

The Saudi Fund for Development agreed $403m in concessional loans under six agreements, Al Jazeera reported, citing the Saudi Press Agency. They include $100m for health facilities and $90m for the Aleppo thermal power plant.
Syria's foreign ministry called the defence deal the most notable agreement but did not disclose its terms. Syria is weighing whether to join a defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan.
The leaders called for an end to actions threatening shipping in the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandeb and the Strait of Hormuz.

stories.head: Israel's president starts coalition talks after election deadlock
stories.say: Isaac Herzog has begun talks with Israel's parties on who should form a government, after the election committee found no fraud and neither Netanyahu nor Gadi Eisenkot won a majority.
stories.stand: Isaac Herzog accepted certified results after the election committee found no fraud; neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's has a majority.
body: Israel's President Isaac Herzog accepted the certified results of the 27 October election on Wednesday and began consulting parties on who should try to form a government.

The Central Elections Committee said it found no evidence of irregularities that compromised the vote or affected its results. Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed, without evidence, that Arab-led parties stole the election.
Al Jazeera reported that Netanyahu's coalition won 53 of the Knesset's 120 seats and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot's bloc 48, with 61 needed to govern. Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats.
Herzog has several days to choose a candidate after the consultations. If no one can form a government, Israel would hold another election early next year.

stories.head: South Korea to move anti-piracy unit closer to Strait of Hormuz
stories.say: South Korea plans to send its anti-piracy naval unit to waters south of Oman, closer to the Strait of Hormuz, adding 75 personnel and a patrol aircraft if parliament agrees.
stories.stand: Seoul plans to extend the Cheonghae Unit's area to waters south of Oman and add 75 personnel, subject to parliamentary approval.
body: South Korea plans to extend its Cheonghae anti-piracy unit's operations from the Gulf of Aden to waters south of Oman, closer to the Strait of Hormuz, the defence ministry said on Thursday.
The unit's personnel ceiling would rise from 320 to 395, the Korea Times reported, adding a P-8 maritime patrol aircraft and a team with unmanned mine-clearing equipment.

The plan needs approval from the cabinet, the president and the National Assembly, and would run to 31 December 2027. The ministry said South Korea would not take part in the war under any circumstances.
The Jerusalem Post reported that Donald Trump has pressed Seoul for more support in the Iran war.

stories.head: Ethiopia expels six Sudanese diplomats and shuts consulate
stories.say: Ethiopia has ordered six Sudanese diplomats out within 48 hours and shut Sudan's consulate in Asosa, as Khartoum accuses the RSF of launching drone attacks from Ethiopian soil.
stories.stand: The move follows Sudanese accusations that the RSF is using Ethiopian territory to launch drone attacks, which Addis Ababa denies.
body: Ethiopia has ordered six Sudanese diplomats to leave within 48 hours and closed Sudan's consulate in the border town of Asosa, according to Ethiopian and Sudanese officials cited by Al Jazeera.

Sudan accuses the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces of using Ethiopian territory to launch drone attacks, and complained to the UN Security Council and the African Union on Sunday. Ethiopia denies backing the RSF.
Ethiopia in turn accuses Sudan's army of supporting rebels linked to the Tigray People's Liberation Front, which Khartoum denies.
Amjad Farid, an adviser to Sudan's Transitional Sovereign Council, said Khartoum would defend its territory but was trying to avoid open war.

stories.head: Libya's eastern parliament names new central bank governor
stories.say: Lawmakers in eastern Libya have appointed Fawzi Abu Khazam to run the country's central bank, with 78 of the 90 members present backing him.
stories.stand: Lawmakers in Benghazi appointed Fawzi Abu Khazam after accepting Naji Issa's resignation; the rival western council has not commented.
body: Libya's eastern-based parliament has appointed Fawzi Abu Khazam as governor of the Central Bank of Libya, after accepting the resignation of Naji Issa.
A parliament spokesperson said 78 of the 90 members present voted for the appointment on Wednesday. Issa, appointed in 2024, submitted his resignation in August without giving public reasons.

Libya is split between a UN-recognised government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east backed by commander Khalifa Haftar. The Tripoli-based High Council of State had not commented on the vote.
Separately, Niger signed a cooperation agreement with Haftar in Benghazi, Africanews reported.

stories.head: Zelensky makes surprise visit to Ibero-American summit in Madrid
stories.say: Volodymyr Zelensky flew into Madrid unannounced on Wednesday for the 30th Ibero-American Summit, where he is due to meet Pedro Sánchez and King Felipe VI.
stories.stand: The Ukrainian president arrived as Spain hosted the 30th summit, where King Felipe VI urged open economies over protectionism.
body: Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Madrid on Wednesday for the 30th Ibero-American Summit, in a visit kept secret for security reasons until his plane landed.
Euronews reported he would hold talks with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and King Felipe VI, and meet representatives of Latin American delegations. He said strengthening air defences was a priority.
Opening the two-day summit, King Felipe VI argued for open economies with equal rules rather than protectionism. Brazil's Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum stayed away.
Honduras will host the next summit in 2028, Infobae reported. Spain's foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, said all 22 member countries had sent at least their foreign minister.

stories.head: Supreme Court hears challenge to Palestine Action ban as protesters held
stories.say: Five Supreme Court justices began hearing a challenge to the Palestine Action ban on Wednesday, as police arrested at least 25 supporters outside the court.
stories.stand: The UK's highest court is weighing whether the 2025 terrorism ban on Palestine Action was lawful; a ruling will come later.
body: The Supreme Court began hearing an appeal on Wednesday against the government's ban on Palestine Action under anti-terrorism laws. The challenge is brought by the group's co-founder, Huda Ammori.
Outside the court, police arrested at least 25 people on suspicion of showing support for a proscribed organisation. Footage showed officers carrying protesters to a police van.

Raza Husain KC, for Ms Ammori, told the five justices that only 3 of the group's 385 actions over five years met the legal definition of terrorism. Sir James Eadie KC, for the Home Office, argued that serious property damage can count as terrorism without violence.

The High Court found the ban unlawful in February, but the Court of Appeal ruled in June that it was lawful and proportionate. Jewish community groups also made submissions supporting the ban. A decision is expected later.

stories.head: Police facial recognition to be put under new law and watchdog
stories.say: The Home Office says police use of facial recognition will need to be intelligence-led and proportionate, with a new watchdog able to stop forces using it.
stories.stand: Ministers will legislate to limit when police can use facial recognition, while funding more live camera vans for England and Wales.
body: The Home Office says police use of facial recognition will be governed by a specific new law. Deployments must be intelligence-led and proportionate, and only where officers believe wanted people could be present.
An independent watchdog will oversee police technology and could stop a force using it if rules are broken. Any system must be independently tested for bias by age, gender and race.
The government is also spending £11m to triple the number of live facial recognition vans in England and Wales. It says a camera pilot in Croydon led to 173 arrests.
A separate legal code will cover shops and other businesses. Simon Randall, chief executive of the firm Pimloc, said the government had not yet spelled out rules on data access and retention.

stories.head: Police posted at Glasgow fire stations for Bonfire Night
stories.say: Twenty officers are being based at ten fire stations around Glasgow on Thursday night, backed by public order officers from 18 English and Welsh forces.
stories.stand: Police Scotland is mounting its largest operation since a 2025 presidential visit to curb firework attacks on emergency crews.
body: Police Scotland says 20 officers will be based at ten fire stations across Glasgow, East Dunbartonshire and East Renfrewshire on 5 November. Public order officers from 18 English and Welsh forces are assisting.
STV reports it is the largest deployment since Donald Trump visited Aberdeenshire in 2025. Glasgow has four firework control zones and a dispersal zone in Pollokshields.
Police received more than 830 reports of disorder over Bonfire Night last year, almost 40% fewer than the year before. The fire service took 750 calls that night.
On Halloween, police responded to 144 firework-related calls, down from 160 a year earlier. Officers said fireworks were thrown at people, vehicles and buildings.

stories.head: Nine men on trial over abuse of woman drugged by her husband
stories.say: Nine men deny sexually abusing a woman whose husband has admitted drugging and raping her for years, as their trial continues at a Manchester court.
stories.stand: The husband has admitted 62 offences; prosecutors say he invited other men to abuse his unconscious wife at their Stockport home.
body: Nine men are on trial at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court accused of sexual offences against a woman who was drugged by her husband. All nine deny the charges.
The husband, a man in his 60s from Stockport, has admitted 62 offences, including rape and administering substances to stupefy his wife. He cannot be named to protect her anonymity.
Prosecutor Louise Oakley KC told jurors he invited other men to the couple's home from 2023 at the latest. Police found more than a million images and videos on a phone, ITV reported.
Four other men have already pleaded guilty in connection with the case. ITV said the trial is expected to last about three months.

stories.say: Two men from Luton have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a 26-year-old Hendon FC midfielder died following an assault in Milton Keynes.
stories.stand: Thames Valley Police are treating the death of the non-league footballer, attacked in the city centre early on Sunday, as murder.
body: A 26-year-old non-league footballer has died after being assaulted in Milton Keynes city centre. Police were called to Midsummer Boulevard shortly before 2am on Sunday, and he died in hospital on Monday.

Thames Valley Police said two men from Luton, aged 21 and 28, were arrested on suspicion of murder. A 30-year-old man from Luton was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender. All three remain in custody.
The victim, from London, joined Hendon FC in September. The club postponed a London Senior Cup tie against Woodford Town.
Detective Inspector Rob Underhill said police did not believe there was any wider risk to the community. Officers are appealing for phone, dashcam or CCTV footage.

stories.head: Lurgan man admits murder of nursing student found by burning car
stories.say: Gary Damien Scullion has changed his plea to guilty at Belfast Crown Court over the murder of a 23-year-old nursing student in Lurgan in December 2023.
stories.stand: The 24-year-old faces a mandatory life sentence; four others in Northern Ireland deny charges linked to the killing.
body: Gary Damien Scullion, 24, of Edward Street, Lurgan, pleaded guilty to murder at Belfast Crown Court on Tuesday. He had denied the charge in November 2024.
The victim, a 23-year-old nursing student from Lurgan, was found beaten and burned beside a car that had been set alight in December 2023.
Mr Justice Fowler said the only sentence available was life imprisonment. A date has not been set for the hearing that will decide his minimum term.
Four co-accused deny charges including murder, assisting offenders and perverting the course of justice. Their case is listed again on 13 November.

stories.head: Man charged with murder after woman found dead in Llandudno
stories.say: A 36-year-old man has been charged with murder after a woman aged 33 was found dead at a house in Llandudno on Halloween night.
stories.stand: North Wales Police charged Christopher Thomas Ellis, who was remanded in custody and sent to Caernarfon Crown Court.
body: North Wales Police have charged Christopher Thomas Ellis, 36, of no fixed address, with murder. A 33-year-old woman was found dead at a property on St Seiriol's Road, Llandudno.
Officers were called shortly after 8pm on Saturday 31 October to reports of a disturbance. Mr Ellis was later arrested near Trinity Avenue in the town.
He appeared at Llandudno Magistrates' Court on Tuesday and was remanded in custody. He was due before Caernarfon Crown Court on Wednesday.
Police are appealing for anyone who was trick-or-treating nearby between 7pm and 8.30pm, or who has dashcam or phone footage, to come forward.

stories.head: September air traffic control failure cost UK about £33m, study finds
stories.say: An analysis by the Cyber Monitoring Centre puts the cost of September's air traffic control failure at about thirty-three million pounds, mostly borne by airlines.
stories.stand: The Cyber Monitoring Centre says a legacy software defect at Nats caused the 8 September outage, which cancelled more than 2,000 flights.
body: The Cyber Monitoring Centre says the air traffic control failure on 8 September cost UK airlines, airports and travel firms about £33m. Airlines bore more than three-quarters of the losses.
The outage at National Air Traffic Services, or Nats, led to more than 2,000 flight cancellations. The centre blamed a previously unknown defect in legacy software and said it was not malicious.
Including overseas airlines, the centre put the global cost at £48m to £76m. It estimated Nats itself lost less than £1m in route charges.
Nats declined to comment while the Civil Aviation Authority carries out an independent review.

stories.head: Eight new stations proposed for Swansea Bay and West Wales rail metro
stories.say: Transport for Wales has proposed eight new stations and extra trains around Swansea, and is asking people whether they would use them.
stories.stand: The plans need further development and UK Government funding; no costs or delivery dates have been given.
body: Transport for Wales has set out plans for the Swansea Bay and West Wales Metro, including eight new stations. A public survey runs until 13 December.
The first phase would add up to two extra trains an hour between Swansea and Pembrey & Burry Port, with a new station at Cockett.
A second phase would run two extra trains an hour from Swansea to Ammanford via Neath. New stations are proposed at Landore, Winsh-wen, Morriston, Llandarcy, Felindre, Pont-lliw and Ammanford.
No costs or delivery dates were given. Railadvent reports that funding would need to come from the UK Government.

stories.head: Scottish police seize more than 1,000 e-bikes and e-scooters this year
stories.say: Police Scotland seized five hundred and sixty-one e-bikes and four hundred and forty-one e-scooters by mid-October, up more than sixty per cent on 2025.
stories.stand: The Scottish Police Federation wants new powers to stop riders, while ministers in Edinburgh say key laws are reserved to Westminster.
body: Police Scotland had seized 561 e-bikes and 441 e-scooters this year by 16 October, according to its figures. That is more than 60% up on 2025.

David Threadgold, chairman of the Scottish Police Federation, said officers' options for dealing with dangerous riders were limited. The federation wants powers to make riders stop and remove face coverings.

Community safety minister Kirsten Oswald said the Scottish Government wants police to be able to seize and keep vehicles used for antisocial behaviour. She said road traffic law is reserved to Westminster.
A UK Government spokesperson said privately owned e-scooters remain illegal on roads and pavements, and that new laws are coming.

stories.head: Government aims to halve homelessness among young care leavers
stories.say: Ministers have launched a plan to halve homelessness among young people leaving care in England, with new duties on councils and three million pounds for prevention.
stories.stand: The plan sets councils new housing duties for care leavers; charities welcomed it but warned it needs enough investment and homes.
body: The government has launched an action plan to halve homelessness among young people leaving care in England. Councils will have to publish plans for care leavers' housing needs.
Care leavers under 25 can no longer be found intentionally homeless. The Department for Education says there are 86,890 care leavers aged 18 to 24 in England, up almost 10% in two years.
The plan includes a £3m programme on preventing youth homelessness. Advisers will give targeted help to councils in higher-risk areas.

The charity Centrepoint says care leavers aged 18 to 20 assessed as facing homelessness rose 37% in five years. Coram welcomed the plan but warned targets need enough investment and affordable housing.

stories.head: Bill gives England's mayors power to charge overnight visitor levy
stories.say: A bill letting mayors in England charge a levy on overnight stays was introduced to the Commons on Wednesday, with ten mayors pledging to keep it at five per cent or less.
stories.stand: The Visitor Levy Bill lets local leaders tax overnight stays; hospitality bosses say it will cost jobs.
body: The Visitor Levy Bill was introduced in the House of Commons on Wednesday. It would let mayors and local leaders in England charge a levy on overnight stays.
The charge would be a percentage of the accommodation cost, applied to the first 28 consecutive days. Ten mayors have committed to keeping it at 5% or below.
Money raised would stay in the area. Student housing, care homes and refuges would be exempt, and leaders must consult before introducing a levy.
The trade body UKHospitality opposes the plans. Citing Oxford Economics, it says a 5% levy would cost 33,000 jobs.

stories.head: Vance blames the Iran war for Republicans' midterm defeat
stories.say: JD Vance says the war with Iran is the reason Republicans lost Congress, while Donald Trump calls it only one factor and says he would do it again.
stories.stand: The vice-president publicly tied the midterm rout to the Iran war; the president partly agreed but defended the decision.
body: Vice-President JD Vance said on Wednesday that the Iran war cost Republicans control of Congress. In a post on X he wrote that the war was the reason the party lost.

He challenged anyone who believed the war was worth losing the Senate to argue so openly. He also cited a pollster's list of tasks for winning voters back, including ending the war, the cost of living and ties with Israel.

Donald Trump said he was fine with Vance's post. He called the war one of several reasons for the defeat, said it was needed to stop Iran getting a nuclear weapon and said he would act the same way again.
Trump also argued that Republicans would have won had he been on the ballot. According to Fox News, unnamed officials said Vance was not breaking with the president.

stories.say: Mike Johnson won't seek to lead House Republicans next year, Hakeem Jeffries is running for Speaker, and Chuck Schumer says he'll be re-elected Senate majority leader.
stories.stand: The midterm result has opened leadership contests in both parties, with Republicans due to vote on 10 November.
body: House Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek to lead Republicans in the next Congress, according to Fox News and NPR, citing sources. Fox said he told staff on a call on Wednesday morning.
Jim Jordan and Steve Scalise are both running for minority leader, Fox reported. NPR said Republican leadership elections are scheduled for 10 November.
Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he would run for Speaker. He promised to work across parties on costs and said the House would act as a check on the executive.
In the Senate, Chuck Schumer said he would be re-elected majority leader. Fox reported that 5 newly elected Democrats, including Abdul El-Sayed, have said they will oppose him.

stories.head: Mississippi Senate race on a knife-edge as ballots are counted
stories.say: Democrat Scott Colom leads Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by a few dozen votes in Mississippi's Senate race, with about 44,000 ballots still to be processed.
stories.stand: Democrat Scott Colom narrowly leads the Republican incumbent with about 44,000 ballots still to process; Alaska's Senate race is also undecided.
body: The Senate race in Mississippi remained uncalled on Wednesday. Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney, led Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by a few dozen votes, CBS News reported.
Fox News put Colom's lead at 43 votes in unofficial results, with about 44,000 absentee, affidavit and provisional ballots still to process. Absentee ballots can arrive until 10 November.
Lawyer Marc Elias said his firm was leading the Democratic legal effort. The state Democratic Party has gone to court over problems at polling places in DeSoto County.
Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982. Alaska's Senate race is also still being counted.

stories.stand: Florida's outgoing governor said the losses were close to an extinction-level event for Republicans, while praising his own state's result.
body: Ron DeSantis, Florida's outgoing governor, said on Wednesday that the midterm losses were close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country.
He said Democrats were unpopular and had not earned a mandate, describing the vote as a rejection of Republicans in Washington. He said regaining unified control could take several election cycles.
DeSantis claimed Florida would be the only one of the 10 largest states with full Republican control. Byron Donalds won the race to succeed him.
He credited a property tax measure, Amendment 3, with drawing voters. Fox News reported it passed with about 62% of the vote.

stories.stand: The first Muslim elected to the US Senate says Trump is right to end military aid to Israel and wants arms sales stopped too.
body: Abdul El-Sayed, who won Michigan's Senate race on Tuesday, said Donald Trump was right to end annual military aid to Israel. He made the remarks in an interview with NPR, The Jerusalem Post reported.
Trump said on Tuesday that he and Israel's prime minister had agreed to end the aid. The current agreement provides $3.8 billion a year until 2028.
El-Sayed called for a complete halt to US arms sales to Israel and a review of military support to several other countries.
El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers and will become the first Muslim US senator. New York mayor Zohran Mamdani said the win meant a great deal to many people.

stories.head: UK agrees to time-bound talks on the harms of the slave trade
stories.say: Britain has agreed to talks with Commonwealth leaders on the historical harms of the slave trade; Andy Burnham is open to a formal apology but rules out reparations.
stories.stand: At the Commonwealth summit in Antigua, the UK agreed to talks on slavery's harms; the prime minister is open to an apology but rejects reparations.
body: The UK has agreed to take part in talks on the historical harms of the transatlantic slave trade, according to a joint statement from Commonwealth leaders meeting in Antigua.

The statement describes the talks as structured, time-bound, inclusive and in good faith. The timetable will be set later, but Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband suggested the process would likely end within a year.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham opened the door to a formal apology but ruled out direct reparations. He said he would look at ways to help poorer countries with debt repayments.
The UK will spend £40 million over three years from existing budgets on Caribbean infrastructure. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch opposes an apology and compensation.

stories.say: Andy Burnham says the US midterm result is a chance for the world to unite around the cost of living, and warns bills won't fall until the Middle East conflict ends.
stories.stand: The prime minister said the US result offered a chance for countries to unite on living costs and called for de-escalation over Iran.
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that the world had an opportunity to unite around the cost of living after the US midterm elections.
Speaking to reporters at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua, he said Donald Trump had accepted the results. He called for a laser-like focus on living costs.
Burnham said he could not bring cost pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East was resolved. He said the UK would push for de-escalation in the Iran conflict.
He also called for the Strait of Hormuz to be fully reopened, according to The News. He said the cost of living had been his top priority in his first three months in office.

stories.stand: A serving RAF wing commander has left the forces to become Reform UK's armed forces spokesman, giving the party eight frontbench spokespeople.
body: Reform UK is to unveil Angus MacIntyre, an RAF wing commander, as its armed forces spokesman on Thursday, the Press Association reported. He has stood down from the RAF to take the role.
MacIntyre joined the Army in 1986 and the RAF Regiment in 1999. He served in Afghanistan, Iraq, Sierra Leone and Somalia, among other places.
Nigel Farage said MacIntyre had more experience than the government's entire defence team. Reform says it would raise defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035.
The appointment gives Reform eight frontbench spokespeople. Labour's Luke Pollard criticised Reform's first-100-days plan for not mentioning the military.

stories.say: With only a small share of districts counted in South Africa's local elections, the ANC is just ahead of the Democratic Alliance, and coalition talks loom.
stories.stand: Early official figures put the ANC slightly ahead of the DA, with about 4% of voting districts counted.
body: Counting is under way after South Africans voted for municipal councils on Wednesday, including 8 big city municipalities, 44 district councils and 205 local councils.
Early Electoral Commission figures compiled by Elections and Seat Projections showed the ANC on 34.8% and the DA on 32.4%, with 4.1% of voting districts counted at 02:35 local time on Thursday.
Johannesburg, run by a fragile ANC-led coalition, is the main battleground, Africanews reported. The DA is targeting the city.
Daily Maverick reported that the ANC must settle coalition partners within about three weeks. The party has said its national leadership will decide coalition deals.

stories.say: Australia's High Court will hear Pauline Hanson's appeal against a finding that she racially vilified Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi, with no date yet set.
stories.stand: The One Nation leader will challenge the validity of Australia's racial discrimination laws after losing in the Federal Court.
body: Australia's High Court has agreed to hear Pauline Hanson's appeal against a finding that she racially vilified Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi, ABC News reported on Thursday.
The case concerns a 2022 post in which Hanson told Faruqi to go back to Pakistan. A Federal Court judge ruled against Hanson in 2024 and the full court dismissed her appeal in July 2026.
Hanson argues the Commonwealth lacked power to make the racial discrimination laws and that they breach the implied freedom of political communication.
The Commonwealth Attorney-General is a respondent alongside Faruqi. No hearing date has been set.

stories.head: French MPs reject the revenue half of the 2027 budget
stories.say: France's National Assembly has voted down the revenue section of next year's budget by 458 votes to none, sending the bill to the Senate.
stories.stand: Every group in the National Assembly voted against the revenue part of Sébastien Lecornu's 2027 budget, so the bill moves to the Senate.
body: France's National Assembly rejected the revenue section of the 2027 budget late on Wednesday by 458 votes to 0, with 2 abstentions, Infobae reported.
Under Assembly rules, the whole bill is treated as rejected at first reading, so the spending section will not be debated. The text now goes to the Senate.
The bill was put forward by Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu's government. Government sources played down the defeat and said they expected a compromise after the Senate reading.

stories.head: Eurozone inflation reaches 4% for first time in three years
stories.say: Prices across the euro area rose four per cent in the year to October, the fastest pace since September 2023, driven by energy costs up more than twenty per cent.
stories.stand: Eurostat's flash estimate puts October inflation at 4.0%, up from 3.8%, as energy prices surged.
body: Annual inflation in the eurozone rose to 4.0% in October from 3.8% in September, according to Eurostat's flash estimate. It is the highest rate since September 2023.
Energy prices were 20.8% higher than a year earlier and added about 1.9 percentage points to the headline rate. Core inflation, which strips out energy and food, held at 2.5%.
Italy saw the sharpest rise, with inflation climbing to 5.6% from 4.2%. Germany's rate eased to 2.8%, helped by a fuel tax cut.
The European Central Bank held its deposit rate at 2.5% on 29 October. Its next meeting is on 16 and 17 December.

body: NASA's Swift Observatory re-entered Earth's atmosphere at 12:39 UTC on Wednesday 4 November, over Sumatra in Indonesia. The US Space Force tracked its descent.
Swift was launched in November 2004 for a two-year study of gamma-ray bursts and exploding stars. CBS News reports it observed more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts before it was switched off in October.
Solar activity dragged the 1.5-tonne craft lower over recent years. A robotic boost mission by Katalyst Space ran into trouble after its July launch and fell back to Earth in September.

body: Astronomers led by Lynn Matthews of MIT Haystack Observatory say a smaller companion star, Siwarha, appears to pass through the outer atmosphere of the red supergiant Betelgeuse.
The team used the Very Large Array in New Mexico and the ALMA array in Chile, observing from 2021 to 2026. The results appear in The Astronomical Journal.

Betelgeuse looks more stretched when the companion is at its widest separation, and rounder when it passes in front of or behind the star. The companion is too faint to see directly at radio wavelengths.
The data also show the star's atmosphere has largely recovered from the Great Dimming of 2019 to 2020. The authors say more observations are needed to confirm the link.

stories.head: X-ray study offers strong evidence for a third kind of magnetism
stories.say: A team led from Stanford's SLAC lab says manganese telluride shows a telltale handedness in its spins, backing the idea of altermagnets, which could suit future data storage.
stories.stand: SLAC-led physicists report experimental evidence that manganese telluride is an altermagnet, a magnetic class first proposed in 2022.
body: Researchers led by SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory report evidence of altermagnetism, a proposed third class of magnetism alongside ferromagnets and antiferromagnets. The paper appears in the journal Science.

The team studied manganese telluride, long classed as an ordinary antiferromagnet. Using circularly polarised X-rays at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in France, they detected a handedness in its magnetic structure.
Lead author Daniel Jost and colleagues ran the experiment in 2024 and repeated it in early 2025 with the same result. Ordinary antiferromagnets should not show this signal, according to SLAC.
The term altermagnet was coined in 2022. Researchers say such materials could offer stable but readable data storage, with possible uses in memory and quantum technology.

stories.stand: LHCb physicists report evidence of a neutral B meson decaying into two muons, a decay sought for more than four decades.
body: Physicists on CERN's LHCb experiment report the first evidence of a neutral B meson decaying into a pair of muons. The Standard Model predicts this happens about once in every 10 billion such particles.
The combined result has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. That counts as evidence but falls short of the five-sigma level usually needed to claim a discovery.
The analysis combined data from 2024 and 2025, taken with the upgraded detector, with data from 2011 to 2018. The University of Birmingham describes it as a milestone in a 42-year search.
The measured rate is close to Standard Model predictions. The findings have been posted as a preprint, and researchers say more data are needed.

stories.head: Iron Age ruler Verica may have been a woman, archaeologist argues
stories.say: An archaeologist at Bournemouth University argues that a British ruler who helped prompt Rome's invasion in AD 43 was probably a queen, not a king, citing coins and the name itself.
stories.stand: Bournemouth University's Miles Russell says coins and Roman sources suggest Verica, ruler of the Atrebates, was a woman rather than a man.
body: Miles Russell, an archaeologist at Bournemouth University, argues that Verica, an Iron Age ruler of the Atrebates in southern England, was probably a woman.
Verica was ousted around AD 40, fled to Rome and is said to have helped persuade Emperor Claudius to invade Britain in AD 43.

Russell points to coins showing a slender, bare-breasted rider, unlike male warriors on other British coins. He says the title rex was used for female rulers too, and notes that names ending in a were common for women.
The argument appears in a new book and in the magazine Current Archaeology. Neither report cites independent experts, and the case rests on interpreting coins and ancient texts.

stories.stand: Judge Leo Sorokin dismissed all charges against Harvard Medical School scientist Kseniia Petrova at prosecutors' request.
body: A federal judge in Boston dismissed all criminal charges on Wednesday against Kseniia Petrova, a Russian-born scientist at Harvard Medical School. Judge Leo Sorokin ruled without a hearing.

Petrova was stopped at Boston Logan airport in early 2025 carrying frog embryo samples from a lab in France for her research. She was later charged with smuggling, concealing facts and making false statements.

US Attorney Leah Foley asked for the dismissal on Tuesday, writing that continuing would cost more than the public interest justified. She called the defence's claims of vindictive prosecution meritless.
In April a judge ruled that a customs officer had improperly cancelled Petrova's visa. Her lawyer, Daniel Marx, said the case should never have been brought.

stories.stand: NASA has unveiled the X-70, a crewed research aircraft for testing new flight-control and manoeuvrability technology, with a first flight expected within two years.
body: NASA unveiled the X-70, nicknamed Fractal, on Wednesday at the UP.Summit event at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. It is the agency's newest experimental X-plane.

NASA says the crewed aircraft can be quickly reconfigured to test advanced flight controls and manoeuvrability. It can carry up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads inside and outside the airframe.

The agency lists a take-off weight of 10,000 pounds, a ceiling of 45,000 feet and a range of about 1,500 nautical miles. Administrator Jared Isaacman expects a first flight under NASA within two years.
NASA has not said who is building the aircraft or what it will cost. The image released with the announcement was generated, not a photograph.

body: NASA announced on Wednesday contracts for three companies to develop Ka-band satellite relay concepts for space communications.
The maximum potential values are $264.3 million for Astranis, $340.4 million for Global Enterprise Solutions and $460.9 million for Viasat, including options.
The first phase runs until May 2027, with options extending work through 2029. NASA can add funding to move from concepts to an in-orbit demonstration.
The agency says the services must work with existing spacecraft without changes to their systems. It plans to retire its Tracking and Data Relay Satellite fleet and rely on commercial providers.

stories.head: MIT team builds new nanoparticle crystals with flexible linkers
stories.say: Engineers found that soft, charged connector molecules can arrange tiny particles into crystal patterns not seen before, overturning a long-held view that linkers must be rigid.
stories.stand: MIT researchers used flexible, charged linker molecules to assemble nanoparticles into previously unseen crystal structures, reported in Nature Materials.
body: Researchers at MIT report a new way to assemble nanoparticles into crystals, using highly flexible connector molecules with electrically charged tips. The work appears in the journal Nature Materials.
For about 20 years, the field had held that such linkers must be rigid for assembly to work, MIT says. Senior author Rob Macfarlane said the opposite extreme works just as well.
Opposite charges attract, so the linkers bend to join up and set how many bonds each particle forms. Changing particle sizes and chain lengths let the team control the result.
The method produced crystal structures not seen before, including less densely packed networks. The researchers say these could be useful for materials that handle light, catalysis or sensing.

stories.head: Grape-sized stone found in 5,300-year-old grave in southern Russia
stories.say: Anthropologists say a Bronze Age cattle herder buried near the Black Sea probably suffered a long-running urinary infection, after finding a stone about two centimetres across.
stories.stand: A 2.1cm stone found in a Bronze Age burial mound points to a chronic urinary infection in a man who died about 5,300 years ago.
body: Researchers have described a grape-sized stone found with the remains of a man buried about 5,300 years ago in a kurgan, or burial mound, in south-western Russia near the Black Sea.
The stone measures about 2.1cm across. X-ray analysis found calcium, phosphorus and whitlockite, a rare mineral linked to kidney, bladder and prostate stones and to bacterial infection.

Lead researcher Natalia Berezina of Lomonosov Moscow State University and colleagues say a kidney stone caused by chronic infection is the most likely explanation. It is unclear whether it contributed to his death.
The man, in his 40s, also had worn joints and healed fractures, which the team links to herding cattle and handling heavy wagons. The study appears in Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences.

stories.head: Rare leprosy strain found in fifth-century boat burial in Germany
stories.say: Genetic tests on a man buried in a boat near the Elbe estuary show he came from the Danube region and carried a form of leprosy never before found in central or northern Europe.
stories.stand: Researchers in Kiel say a man buried in a boat at Fallward carried a leprosy strain not previously detected in central or northern Europe.
body: Researchers in Germany say a man buried in a boat in the fifth century AD, near the mouth of the Elbe on the North Sea coast, carried a very rare form of leprosy.
The study, led by teams at Kiel University and the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research, appears in the journal iScience.

Genetic analysis indicates the man came from the Danube region. The leprosy strain belongs to a group previously known from Egypt between the fourth and second centuries BC, and not detected in central or northern Europe.
His bones showed no damage from the disease. The researchers suggest he may have been a mercenary in the Roman army or a long-distance trader.

body: Field researchers have reported rock paintings estimated to be about 5,000 years old in natural cave shelters in Tamil Nadu, southern India.
The images show human figures, wild animals, dancing and geometric designs. They are thought to date from the shift from hunting and gathering to early farming.

Heritage enthusiasts have asked the Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology and the Archaeological Survey of India to list the site as a protected monument. Reports do not name the exact location or the discoverers.

stories.head: Cocaine overtakes heroin in drug deaths in England and Wales
stories.say: Cocaine was involved in more than twelve hundred deaths registered in England and Wales in 2025, overtaking heroin for the first time, though total drug deaths fell slightly.
stories.stand: Cocaine was the substance most often mentioned in drug poisoning deaths registered in 2025, the first time since records began in 1993.
body: Cocaine was involved in 1,233 drug poisoning deaths registered in England and Wales in 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics. Heroin or morphine was involved in 1,210.
It is the first time cocaine has been the most frequently mentioned substance since the series began in 1993. Opiates and opioids as a group remained the most common, with 2,324 deaths.
Overall, 5,519 drug poisoning deaths were registered, down from 5,565 in 2024. The rate fell to 92.4 per million, the first annual fall since 2012.
Wales had a rate of 141.3 per million, against 89.5 in England. The ONS said 62.7% of deaths registered in 2025 occurred in earlier years, because of inquest delays.

body: The World Health Organization approved clinical trials of 2 new Ebola vaccine candidates on Wednesday, Africanews reported. Both were developed for the Bundibugyo virus behind the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

One, ChAdOx1 BDBV, was developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India. The other, mRNA-1469, was developed by Moderna. They join a trial led by Congo's National Institute for Biomedical Research.
The existing vaccine Ervebo is approved for a different Ebola virus. Africa CDC figures put the outbreak at 10,444 confirmed cases and more than 5,300 deaths.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said vaccines did not replace measures such as contact tracing, isolation and safe burials.

stories.say: Eighty-five health and environmental groups have asked the World Health Organization to review its limit on nitrate in drinking water, which dates back to 1958.

body: A coalition of 85 health and environmental organisations has written to the World Health Organization, Euronews reported. They want it to review its limit on nitrate in drinking water.
The current limit of 50 mg per litre dates from 1958. It was set to prevent blue-baby syndrome, a condition that reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen.
The groups, including Greenpeace International and the World Organization of Family Doctors, cite studies linking long-term, low-level exposure to bowel cancer and premature birth.
A Danish government-commissioned panel recommended a limit of 6.0 mg per litre last year. No response from the WHO was reported.

stories.head: Swapping dairy for plant-based alternatives may cut iodine intake
stories.say: Replacing milk, cheese and yoghurt with plant-based versions could leave many people short of iodine, calcium and vitamin B12, according to UK researchers.
stories.stand: A UK modelling study found replacing milk, cheese and yoghurt with plant-based products lowered intake of 4 key micronutrients, especially iodine.
body: Replacing dairy foods with plant-based alternatives could leave more people short of key nutrients, a UK study suggests. It was led by the University of Surrey with Queen's University Belfast.
Researchers modelled diet data from more than 3,500 people aged 18 months to 100 years. Even partial swaps caused marked falls in iodine, calcium, riboflavin and vitamin B12.
Mandatory fortification of the alternatives prevented falls in most nutrients, but iodine intake remained inadequate in 59% of adolescent girls. Adding iodine-fortified bread cut that figure to 37%.
The study was published in The Lancet Planetary Health. Lead author Sarah Bath said the UK has no iodine fortification policy such as iodised salt.

body: Researchers at Japan's RIKEN institute say they have found a way to make cancer cells produce a compound that damages them. The method exploits their high levels of carbon monoxide.
The team delivered a palladium-based catalyst, wrapped in the blood protein albumin, into cells. In cancer cells it reacted with carbon monoxide to make phenanthridinone, a toxic compound.
Lab tests used human liver, cervical, breast and lung cancer cells. The compound formed in cancer cells but not in a non-cancerous cell line, and it did not form in blood.
The work, published in Nature Communications, has not yet been tested in animals. Team leader Katsunori Tanaka's group plans animal studies.

stories.head: Studies raise doubts over 'three-parent' IVF for mitochondrial disease
stories.say: New data suggest a mother's faulty mitochondria can sometimes reappear in children born through so-called three-parent IVF, raising questions about the technique.
stories.stand: Data show some mothers' faulty mitochondria can reappear in children born after mitochondrial replacement, prompting calls for caution.
body: New data are raising questions about mitochondrial replacement therapy, the IVF technique sometimes called three-parent IVF, STAT reported.
The method combines parents' DNA with healthy donor mitochondria. But studies show some of the mother's mitochondria can persist or return, a process known as reversion.
Of 8 healthy children born after the treatment in Newcastle, 3 showed low reversion of between 5% and 16%, with no signs of disease. The technique is banned in the US.
Embryologist Jacques Cohen wants a moratorium on its use to prevent disease. Monash University's Mary Herbert said it should be described as reducing risk rather than preventing disease.

body: Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has announced a special health authority to employ NHS England's regional staff outside the civil service, The Telegraph reported.

Ministers had pledged to halve the combined workforce of NHS England and the department, then about 19,000. Baroness Merron told the Lords the 50% cut was an ambition rather than a fixed target.

body: Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration approved Novo Nordisk's Wegovy tablet on Tuesday, ABC News reported. It is the first oral GLP-1 medicine cleared in Australia for weight management.
The regulator registered 4 strengths, from 1.5mg to 25mg. The tablet is taken once a day and requires a prescription.

It is not yet available, as the regulator still has to review packaging and production. No price has been set, and the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme subsidises weight-loss drugs only for people with type 2 diabetes.
Trials found about 14% body weight loss with the tablet, compared with about 15% for the injection.

stories.say: Some 125 new scanners added in England over two years are supporting about a million extra CT and MRI scans a year, according to the government.
stories.stand: The government says 125 new CT and MRI scanners added in England since 2024 support about 1 million extra scans a year.
body: The government says 125 more CT and MRI scanners were added in England between March 2024 and March 2026. It says they support about 1 million extra scans a year.
Of these, 107 went into community diagnostic centres, which carried out nearly 2.2 million scans in the year to March 2026.
AI software to speed up scans is installed in 54% of compatible NHS MRI machines, with an average 14% increase in scans. Every trust will be able to upgrade compatible scanners by 2029.
Health minister Karin Smyth said quick diagnosis can make all the difference for cancer and other serious conditions.

stories.say: Women in Spain whose menopause-related conditions stop them working will be able to take paid sick leave from the first of December.
stories.stand: From 1 December, women whose menopause-related conditions stop them working can take sick leave paid from the second day.

Menopause alone will not qualify. A doctor must diagnose a related condition that temporarily prevents the woman from working.
The employer pays the first day. Social Security then pays 60% of the base for the first 20 days, rising to 75% from day 21. The usual contribution requirement is waived.
Minister Elma Saiz said the government was responding to situations that had been made invisible. Spain introduced leave for incapacitating period pain in 2023.

stories.head: UK bill would end new North Sea licences and scrap gas standing charges
stories.say: Ministers want to write a ban on new North Sea oil and gas exploration into law, and scrap gas standing charges, under a bill introduced on Wednesday.
stories.stand: The Energy Independence Bill puts a ban on new oil and gas exploration licences into law alongside measures the government says will cut bills.
body: The UK government introduced its Energy Independence Bill to Parliament on Wednesday 4 November. It would end new licences to explore for oil and gas fields in the North Sea. Production from existing areas would continue.

The bill would also scrap gas standing charges. The government says around 60% of gas account holders would save an average of £45 a year. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the changes would lower bills.

New Transitional Energy Certificates would allow extra production near licensed areas, which the government says could unlock around 60 million barrels. A £2 billion Energy Wealth Fund and a North Sea Jobs Service are planned for workers.

Shadow Energy Secretary Andrew Bowie said the Conservatives would oppose the move, the Scottish Daily Express reports. Offshore Energies UK urged a focus on energy security, saying Britain imports over 40% of its energy.

stories.head: Six climate and health measures could save 1.6 million lives a year, WHO says
stories.say: The World Health Organization says heat warnings, clean water, sanitation, cleaner cooking fuels and fossil fuel pricing could prevent 1.6 million deaths a year.
stories.stand: A WHO analysis released before the COP31 summit says the six measures would also bring trillions of dollars in benefits each year.
body: The World Health Organization says six climate and health measures could prevent 1.6 million deaths a year if scaled up worldwide. That is about one in every 40 deaths.
The measures are heat-health warning systems, climate-resilient drinking water, basic sanitation, hygiene and handwashing facilities, cleaner household fuels, and more efficient fossil fuel pricing.
The report, released on Wednesday 4 November, estimates US$5.4 trillion a year in fiscal benefits from fossil fuel pricing. WHO says heat-health warnings return US$835 for every US$1 invested.
Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said much of the harm from the climate crisis can be prevented with existing tools. The report comes ahead of the COP31 climate summit.

stories.stand: Environmental groups say energy costs shaped the vote, but Democrats lack the majorities needed to override a presidential veto.
body: Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections. Inside Climate News reports they also gained a majority of governorships for the first time in more than a decade.

House Democrats plan oversight of EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin over staff and science cuts, according to Inside Climate News. Experts quoted by Euronews expect scrutiny of new drilling, methane emissions and fossil fuel subsidies.
Democrats lack a veto-proof majority. President Donald Trump can veto legislation, and overriding him needs two-thirds of both chambers.

stories.stand: Singapore's environment minister says the status quo is no longer tenable after smoke from Indonesian fires spread across the region.
body: Singapore plans to amend its transboundary haze law to widen investigation powers, Environment Minister Grace Fu said on Wednesday 4 November.

Proposed fines would rise to up to S$1 million a day, with a maximum of S$20 million. The current cap is S$2 million. The government could also appoint private-sector assessors to investigate companies.
Singapore has sent notices to 10 Singapore-registered companies over possible links to the haze. ABC News reports the smoke came from fires mainly in Sumatra and Kalimantan in Indonesia.

body: The government is creating eight regional water councils in England, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said on Thursday 5 November. One will cover the Thames region, including London.
The councils will bring together mayors or council leaders with customers, farmers and businesses. They are meant to influence billions of pounds of investment in water and flood infrastructure.
Priorities include sewage, flooding, drought and future supplies. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said local people would for the first time have a real say over their water company.
Mayors will get new powers to hold water companies to account. Environment Secretary Angela Eagle is writing to mayors about the plans, City AM reports.

body: Canberra's largest battery storage system is now online at Williamsdale, south of Tuggeranong, ABC News reported on Thursday 5 November.

body: 3M has agreed to pay up to US$7.35 billion to settle personal injury claims over PFAS, the so-called forever chemicals. The company announced the deal on Tuesday.
The claims centre on firefighting foam used near military bases, airports and other sites. Claimants say groundwater contamination made them ill. Up to about 120,000 plaintiffs are eligible.

body: Researchers say a koala population near Newcastle, New South Wales, may be free of chlamydia, ABC News reported on Thursday 5 November.
No evidence of the disease was found in 27 wild koalas tested in the Sugarloaf-Stockrington State Conservation Area. A review of records for 27 more koalas nearby also found none.
Drone surveys and modelling suggest about 2,300 koalas may live in the area. The work was led by Dr Ryan Witt of the University of Newcastle, with Aboriginal lead Daryn McKenny.
Chlamydia is widespread in NSW koalas. Professor Mark Krockenberger of the University of Sydney said full disease-freedom cannot yet be confirmed.

body: Brazil's COP30 presidency has published a voluntary roadmap to halt and reverse forest loss and degradation by 2030, Carbon Brief reports. It was launched in Brasília on Tuesday 3 November.
The roadmap says about $300bn a year is needed by 2030. Current finance covers less than a third of that, it says, and it offers 10 proposals to raise more.
It sits outside formal UN negotiated outcomes and contains no new commitments. Russia does not support a universal roadmap, according to Carbon Brief.
Brazil says its deforestation rate has fallen by more than 70% since 2022. The launch came less than a week before the COP31 climate summit.

stories.say: Hackers tried to push storage temperatures at three plasma sites run by France's blood service to extreme levels on Monday, but staff stepped in and no products were lost.
stories.stand: Hackers changed temperature settings at three French plasma storage sites, but the national blood service says no products were lost.
body: France's national blood service, the EFS, says hackers raised temperature and defrosting thresholds at 3 of its plasma cold-storage sites on Monday.

Le Canard Enchaîné, which first reported the attack, said storage normally kept at about minus 30C was to be reset as high as 110C. The EFS said monitoring systems spotted the change quickly and staff acted in time.
The service said no blood products or samples were lost and there were no health consequences. Plasma bags were moved or secured, and collection and distribution continued.

The attack hit refrigeration supplier Coolworld, which blamed a component from a third-party supplier. France's national cybersecurity agency and the health ministry are investigating. Supermarket freezers in several European countries were hit in mid-October.

body: Security firm Sekoia says a hacking group it links to Russia's foreign intelligence service infected iPhones and Android phones through compromised and fake websites.

Sekoia attributes the campaign to APT29, also known as Midnight Blizzard or Cozy Bear, with moderate to high confidence. Visitors' devices were profiled and served exploits with no action needed from the user.

Hijacked sites included a Ukrainian gas producer, a US chemical industry trade association and a Bulgarian military-related organisation. Fake sites imitated America250 and the Raffles London hotel. A Ukrainian analytics service, Plerdy, was also compromised.
Apple and Google had patched all the flaws used before the campaign began. Sekoia says users with up-to-date software are safe, and the malware did not survive a reboot.

body: Google says it has disrupted a botnet called XCPE that ran on more than 1.3 million Android TV streaming boxes.

It attributes the backdoor with high confidence to Videostrong, a Shenzhen-based manufacturer. Google says the company built it into firmware and sold access to criminals for ad fraud and residential proxy services.

The takedown does not remove the malware, which sits in the firmware. Researchers say owners may need clean firmware, to disconnect the device or to replace it.

stories.say: Revolut says running AI coding models on its own hardware, rather than paying commercial providers, has cut those costs by about ninety per cent in under a year.
stories.stand: The UK fintech has switched its engineers to an open-weights Chinese model running on its own hardware, an infrastructure lead says.
body: Revolut has made self-hosted AI models the default for its software engineers, cutting AI coding costs by about 90% in under a year, according to an infrastructure lead.
David Abitbol told an AI engineering conference in New York in October that about 2,000 engineers use the tools. The Register, which reported the remarks, notes the figures are his own claims.
Revolut runs GLM models from Chinese developer Z.ai on 56 Nvidia B200 chips. It previously used commercial services including Google's Gemini and Anthropic's Claude Code.
Abitbol said some engineers had been spending up to $10,000 a month with little return. He said privacy concerns about Chinese models mainly apply to remote access, not in-house hosting.

stories.head: OpenAI offers to cut data centre power use when grids are strained
stories.say: OpenAI says its data centres will use less electricity when local grids are under strain, with a planned campus in Georgia offering up to a thousand megawatts of flexibility.
stories.stand: Its Grid Protectors programme would have AI campuses reduce demand during peaks, starting with a planned site in Georgia.
body: OpenAI has announced a programme under which its data centres would reduce electricity use when utilities face high demand or grid emergencies.
The Grid Protectors programme was announced on Monday, according to the trade publication tEDmag. How much and how quickly demand is cut would be agreed locally with utilities and regulators.

A planned campus in Effingham County, Georgia, will be the pilot. OpenAI's agreement with Georgia Power includes up to 1,000MW of flexible demand, which OpenAI says equals average demand of about 700,000 households.

OpenAI says it will pay the full infrastructure and electricity service costs of the Georgia project. Georgia Power projects about $950m in annual customer savings from 2029 from its large-load agreements.

stories.stand: Files and photos shared with anyone holding a link will lose end-to-end encryption and may be reviewed, under changes in iOS 27.3.
body: Apple says photos and files shared through iCloud's Anyone with the Link option will be checked for harmful content.
The change comes with iOS 27.3 and matching updates for iPad, Mac and Vision Pro, now in developer testing. MacRumors says public release is expected in December.

According to an Apple support document, publicly shared items will not be end-to-end encrypted, even for users with Advanced Data Protection. MacRumors reports that links limited to chosen people are not checked.
Apple says it may remove harmful uploads, disable accounts or involve law enforcement. It has not defined harmful content.

stories.say: Nintendo's main supplier of memory chips for Switch game cards is pulling out of that business, though an analyst says physical games will carry on for some time.
stories.stand: Macronix is phasing out its ROM chip business as it shifts to NAND memory, raising questions over physical Switch games.
body: Macronix, which makes the read-only memory chips used in Nintendo Switch game cards, is phasing out that business, according to an analyst and its chairman.
MST Financial analyst David Gibson said on Tuesday that the company will release no new ROM products. Chairman Miin Wu told the Taipei Times the exit would be gradual, Power Up Gaming reports.
ROM made up about 5% of Macronix sales last quarter, as the company shifts towards NAND storage, where data centre demand is strong.
Gibson said Macronix is not Nintendo's only supplier and expects more game-key cards and digital releases. A Nintendo executive said in October the company had no plans to drop physical games.

stories.head: Conductor Herbert Blomstedt dies aged 99
stories.say: Herbert Blomstedt, who led the San Francisco Symphony for a decade and was still conducting this year, died at his home in Gothenburg on Wednesday, aged ninety-nine.
stories.stand: The conductor, whose career spanned seven decades and orchestras across Europe and the US, died at home in Sweden.
body: Herbert Blomstedt, one of the longest-serving conductors in classical music, died at his home in Gothenburg, Sweden, on Wednesday 4 November. He was 99.
His management agency, KünstlerSekretariat am Gasteig, announced the death. No cause was given. OperaWire reported that his family was with him.

Born in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1927 to Swedish parents, he grew up in Sweden. He was music director of the San Francisco Symphony from 1985 to 1995 and chief conductor of the Staatskapelle Dresden from 1975 to 1985.
He also held posts in Norrköping, Oslo and at Danish and Swedish radio orchestras, and won Grammy awards in 1993 and 1996. His final concert was with the San Francisco Symphony in May 2026.

stories.head: Caligula director Tinto Brass dies aged 93
stories.say: The Italian film-maker Tinto Brass, best known for directing Caligula and for decades of erotic cinema, has died at ninety-three, his family announced on Wednesday.
stories.stand: The Milan-born director moved from early experimental films to the erotic cinema that made his name, including the disputed epic Caligula.
body: The Italian director Tinto Brass has died aged 93. His family announced the death on Wednesday 4 November, according to the Italian news agency Ansa. Euronews reported that he died in Rome.
Born in Milan in 1933, he began directing in the 1960s. His debut, In capo al mondo, ran into censorship and was renamed Chi lavora è perduto.

He became known for erotic films including Salon Kitty and Caligula, which starred Malcolm McDowell and was financed by Penthouse founder Bob Guccione. Brass objected to explicit scenes Guccione added after filming and sought to have his name removed.
His wife, Caterina Varzi, described a moment of deep sadness, Euronews reported. No cause of death was given.

stories.head: German children's author Janosch dies aged 95
stories.say: Janosch, the German author and illustrator behind The Trip to Panama and the stripy Tiger Duck, has died at ninety-five at his home on Tenerife, his publisher said.
stories.stand: Horst Eckert, who wrote as Janosch, created picture-book characters loved by generations of German children.
body: The German children's author and illustrator Janosch has died aged 95. His publisher and literary agent, Bernhard Feil, told AFP he died at his home on Tenerife on Tuesday 3 November.
Janosch was the pen name of Horst Eckert, who was born in 1931 in Upper Silesia, then part of Germany and now in Poland.
His best-known book, The Trip to Panama, published in 1978, follows Little Bear and Little Tiger. He also created the Tiger Duck, a striped wooden toy duck on wheels.
Since the 1970s he wrote and illustrated more than 300 books, novels and plays, according to Sweden Herald. His work has been translated into more than 30 languages, A News reported.

stories.say: A UNESCO advisory body has recommended adding shodo, Japanese calligraphy, to its intangible heritage list, with a final decision due at a meeting in China from late November.
stories.stand: If approved in December, shodo would become Japan's 24th entry on UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list.
body: A UNESCO evaluation body has recommended that shodo, the Japanese art of calligraphy, be added to the list of intangible cultural heritage, Japan's Agency for Cultural Affairs said.
UNESCO's intergovernmental committee will make the final decision at a meeting in Xiamen, China, from 30 November to 5 December.
If approved, shodo would be Japan's 24th item on the list. Japan applied in March 2024, but its nominations are effectively reviewed only every two years, so the bid was resubmitted.
Japan is also seeking listings for kagura, a form of sacred dance, and for its hot spring culture, Nippon.com reported.

body: The celebrity hairstylist John Frieda has died aged 75. His salon announced the death on Instagram on Tuesday, saying he died peacefully surrounded by his family. No cause was given.
Born in London in 1951, he created the bowl cut Joanna Lumley wore in The New Avengers in 1976, the year he opened his own salon, Starts at 60 reported.
He co-created the Frizz Ease haircare range and in 2002 sold his haircare company to the Japanese group Kao for US$450 million. His clients included Princess Diana and Madonna.
He was first married to the singer Lulu. He is survived by his wife, four children and two grandchildren.

body: Pixies have released four tracks recorded between 1987 and 1991 on streaming platforms for the first time, NME and Hot Press reported.

stories.stand: Liverpool's first Champions League defeat of the season leaves them on nine points after four games.
body: Fenerbahce beat Liverpool 3-2 in the Champions League in Istanbul on Wednesday, coming from behind twice.

body: Manchester City beat RB Leipzig 3-2 in the Champions League in Germany on Wednesday, with Erling Haaland scoring the winner in the 78th minute.
City led through a Castello Lukeba own goal before Ridle Baku equalised. Enzo Fernandez restored City's lead, but Antonio Nusa levelled again three minutes later.

stories.stand: Cesc Fabregas's side scored the most goals by an away team in the competition's history and moved up to fourth.
body: Como beat Lens 9-1 in France on Wednesday, equalling the largest winning margin in the Champions League era.

stories.say: Real Madrid trailed twice in Athens on Wednesday before Federico Valverde struck in stoppage time to beat AEK three-two, keeping their Champions League record perfect.

stories.head: 1980 Formula One world champion Alan Jones dies aged 80
stories.say: Alan Jones, who won the 1980 Formula One title with Williams, has died at 80 after a short illness, his wife said. He won 12 grands prix before retiring in 1986.
stories.stand: The Australian was one of only two drivers from his country to win the Formula One world championship.
body: Alan Jones, the Australian who won the 1980 Formula One world championship, has died aged 80, three days after his birthday.
His wife, Amanda Butler-Davis, announced his death in a statement and said he had died after a short illness. She said he had dedicated his life to motorsport.
Jones drove for Williams from 1978 and won 12 grands prix, five of them in his title-winning season. He and Sir Jack Brabham are Australia's only Formula One world champions.
He retired in 1986. He later worked as a television commentator on Formula One, including for Channel Nine from 1987 to 2002, ABC News said.

stories.head: Brazilian youth match brawl ends with a record 53 red cards
stories.say: A referee in Brazil showed fifty-three red cards after a mass brawl at an under-20 semi-final in Minas Gerais, beating the previous record of thirty-six set in Argentina in 2011.
stories.stand: Players, coaching staff and club board members were sent off after a fight at the end of an under-20 semi-final.
body: A referee showed 53 red cards after a mass brawl at an under-20 match in Brazil's Minas Gerais state, according to reports.

The match between Uberlandia and Mamore was the first leg of a state under-20 semi-final. Reuters, reported by Yahoo Sports, said 43 players, eight coaching staff and two Uberlandia board members were sent off.
The fight broke out after Mamore scored late to lead 3-1. The referee wrote in his report that he ended the match because of the turmoil and lack of security.
Uberlandia withdrew from the second leg, sending Mamore to the final. The previous record of 36 red cards was set in an Argentine fifth-division match in 2011.

body: Real Madrid have proposed Rafael Nadal, the retired 22-time Grand Slam champion, as a new member of the club's board of directors.
The club said on Wednesday that its board had agreed to put the appointment to the general assembly of delegate members for ratification. No date for the vote was given.

Al Jazeera said Nadal, who retired in November 2024, has played down suggestions he could one day succeed club president Florentino Perez.

stories.head: Owono speaks of hardest days of his life after De Miguel's death
stories.say: Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono said on Wednesday that these were the hardest days of his life, after his collision with Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel, who died on Tuesday.
stories.stand: The goalkeeper's first public words came as Spanish police carry out a standard investigation into the death.
body: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono said he was going through the most difficult days of his life, in a statement released by his club on Wednesday.
Owono collided with Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel during a second-tier Spanish match on Monday. De Miguel, 30, suffered a cardiac arrest and died in hospital on Tuesday.
Owono said he was struggling to process what had happened and would face any questions with respect. He deactivated his Instagram account after receiving abuse online, ESPN and ABC News reported.

Spanish police have opened what ESPN described as a standard investigation. ESPN said the local chief prosecutor told the EFE agency that criminal proceedings were unlikely. De Miguel's funeral is due on Thursday.

stories.head: Hijikata beats Djokovic in Paris, ending his ATP Finals hopes
stories.say: Australian qualifier Rinky Hijikata came from a set down to beat Novak Djokovic in Paris, ending Djokovic's hopes of reaching the ATP Finals in Turin.
stories.stand: Djokovic needed to reach the Paris Masters semi-finals to have a chance of qualifying for the season-ending event.
body: Rinky Hijikata beat Novak Djokovic 2-6, 6-3, 6-3 in the second round of the Paris Masters, his first win over the 24-time Grand Slam champion.

Djokovic needed to reach the semi-finals to keep alive his chance of qualifying for the eight-player ATP Finals in Turin. Yahoo Sports said he took a medical timeout for a shoulder problem in the second set.
Hijikata, an Australian qualifier, said he had not been close to Djokovic's level in the first set. He hit 37 winners, ABC News said.
Alex de Minaur also lost, 7-6, 6-3 to Tomas Martin Etcheverry, leaving him needing a withdrawal to reach Turin. Lorenzo Musetti beat world number one Alexander Zverev.

stories.head: RFU backs Borthwick to lead England at 2027 World Cup
stories.say: The RFU's chief executive Bill Sweeney says Steve Borthwick will lead England at next year's World Cup whatever happens this month, with his contract now running to mid-2028.
stories.stand: Bill Sweeney spoke before England's Nations Championship opener against Australia at Allianz Stadium on Sunday.
body: The Rugby Football Union's chief executive, Bill Sweeney, said he could not envisage Steve Borthwick not leading England at the 2027 World Cup in Australia.
Sweeney said there were no plans to change coach regardless of results against Australia, Japan and New Zealand this month. He said Borthwick's contract had been extended to the middle of 2028.
He called the last Six Nations difficult and said he was very disappointed, but that a review had addressed some problems. He named discipline as a major issue.

stories.say: The ICC says India against Pakistan at next year's Cricket World Cup has drawn eight point four million ticket requests for about thirty-four thousand seats, more than the final.
stories.stand: Total ticket requests for the 2027 tournament in southern Africa have passed 120 million, the ICC says.
body: The India v Pakistan group match at the 2027 Cricket World Cup has drawn more ticket requests than the final, the International Cricket Council said.
The ICC said the game at the Wanderers in Johannesburg on 10 October had 8.4 million requests for about 34,000 seats. The final, also in Johannesburg, drew nearly 8 million.
Total requests have passed 120 million from fans in 193 countries, the ICC said. The tournament runs from 7 October to 21 November 2027 in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.
